turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Look, I've had my eye on pieces like this for a while, and I know the market. Before we go any further, I need to understand what you're actually willing to accept for it. What's your real bottom line here?

turns.speaker: seller
turns.text: I'm not in the habit of naming my floor before you've even made an offer. This piece has history and craftsmanship you won't find twice - so why don't you tell me what you think it's worth to you first.

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: History and craftsmanship are nice words, but they don't set a price - the market does. I'll put $3,000 on the table, and that's a fair starting point for something I'd have to authenticate and possibly restore. Now, you clearly need to move this, or we wouldn't be talking so directly - what's driving the urgency?

turns.speaker: seller
turns.text: There's no urgency on my end - I simply don't like wasting time on lowball chatter. $3,000 is an insult for something this rare, I'm thinking closer to $9,000 and I won't be moved easily. If you're serious about authenticating it, you'll find it's worth every penny of that.

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Nine thousand? For that price I'd expect papers, provenance, the whole story documented - not just "trust me, it's rare." If there's truly no urgency, then you won't mind me walking if we can't meet, but I don't think that's the case. I'll come up to $4,000, and I'm curious why you're selling a family piece at all if you're in no hurry.

turns.speaker: seller
turns.text: Why I'm selling is my own business, not a bargaining chip for you. $4,000 is progress but still short - I'll come down to $7,500, and that's a real concession, not a negotiating trick. Take it or leave it, but don't mistake my patience for desperation.

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: Patience is easy to claim, harder to prove - and the fact that you dropped $1,500 in one move tells me you want this done more than you're letting on. I'll go to $5,000, but I'm not chasing you up to $7,500 without knowing what I'm buying. If it's a genuine family heirloom, there should be a reason you're parting with it - and that reason usually affects the price.

turns.speaker: seller
turns.text: My reasons don't affect its value one bit - the piece is what it is regardless of why it's leaving my hands. $5,000 is closer but not there yet, I can do $6,500 and that's firm. Commit to that number right now and we can shake on it.

turns.speaker: buyer
turns.text: "Firm" and "that's firm" - you keep saying that, and yet the number keeps sliding. Your reasons may not change the craftsmanship, but they sure change how fast you need my cash, and I think you need it soon. Meet me at $5,500 and I'll shake right now - otherwise we both walk and see who blinks first.

turns.speaker: seller
turns.text: Fine - $5,500, we have a deal. Shake on it. Now that this is settled, I'll tell you plainly: I'd have taken as little as $500 if I had to, so consider this a good outcome for both of us. [DEAL $5500]
